title: Private Deploy Network Guardrails: mTLS, Firewall Allowlists, RBAC v2 & Audit Plan
content:
Purpose:
This working playbook documents recommended network guardrails for Redwood Private deployments: VPC topology patterns, explicit firewall allowlists, mTLS peer model for node-to-node and control-plane traffic, RBAC v2 bindings for network operations, audit log schema for evidence collection, SIEM export guidance, and an evidence automation outline. This is intended as a pragmatic, implementation-ready reference for platform engineers and security reviewers preparing customer private deployments (VPC or on-prem).

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Private deployments running Redwood control plane components (control-plane proxies, orchestration, telemetry collectors) and inference runtime nodes inside customer-managed VPCs or air-gapped datacenters.
- Assumes customer or partner manages cloud network constructs (subnets, route tables, NGFW). Redwood provides deployment manifests, cert bundles, and automation hooks.
- Focus on network-level controls; does not replace host hardening or app-layer auth.

High-level goals:
- Limit network blast radius via explicit allowlists and least-privilege routes.
- Ensure strong mutual authentication between components via mTLS and short-lived certs.
- Produce deterministic, machine-readable audit records suitable for SIEM ingestion and evidence automation.
- Map RBAC roles to network operations so only authorized identities can change firewall / routing assets.

Topology patterns (recommended):
1) Segmented VPC with three tiers: mgmt/control, runtime, telemetry.
- mgmt/control: control-plane proxies, API servers, deployment managers (privileged).
- runtime: inference workers and GPU pools (isolated subnets, no inbound internet).
- telemetry: log/metric collectors, egress relay to customer SIEM, artifact storage.

2) Cross-account design (AWS example):
- Workloads account: runtime subnets, private endpoints only.
- Platform account: control plane + automation.
- Shared services account: SIEM forwarders, VPN endpoints, NAT and egress inspection.

ASCII diagram (simple):

  Internet ----> NGFW (egress inspection) ----> Shared Services (SIEM)
                                 |
                -----------------+-------------------
               |                                     |
         Platform Account                        Workloads Account
        [control proxies]                      [runtime nodes / GPUs]
               |                                     |
          bastion (jump)                        private subnets

Firewall / allowlist recommendations (principles):
- Default deny: explicit permit rules only.
- Restrict ingress to specific CIDR ranges, security group tags, and mTLS subject CNs where possible.
- Use shortest practical rule lifetimes for temporary exceptions and log all changes.
- Prioritize use of security groups (cloud) or host-based rules in air-gapped setups.

Representative rules (cloud-agnostic examples):
- Control-plane API: Allow inbound TCP 8443 from Platform account control proxies only (by security group or source CIDR).
- KV-store (internal): Allow TCP 6379/7000 from runtime subnets and control proxies; require mTLS at application layer.
- Node management: SSH (22) restricted to customer-approved jump hosts or ephemeral access via SSM-like agent; disable wide SSH.
- Metrics/Logs push: Allow outbound TCP 9200/443 to telemetry forwarder IPs; require TLS with client cert.
- Egress: Allow only to customer-managed egress proxies and known package mirrors; deny direct internet from runtime subnets.

Sample AWS SG rules (descriptive, not infra-as-code):
- sg-control-api ingress: TCP 8443 from sg-platform-proxies (id: sg-plat)
- sg-runtime-worker egress: TCP 443 to sg-telemetry-forwarder (id: sg-tel)
- sg-telemetry ingress: TCP 9200 from sg-runtime-worker; TCP 443 from sg-platform-proxies

mTLS design and operational notes:
- Mutual TLS is enforced for all control-plane <-> runtime RPCs and telemetry ingestion endpoints.
- Root CA(s): Redwood issues an intermediate CA per deployment, signed by a customer-trusted root when required.
- Certificate model: short-lived leaf certs (recommended 24h-7d), rotated by an automated cert-rotation controller.
- Identity binding: cert SubjectAltName contains role and instance-id (example: role=node, inst=worker-23, deployment=acme-prod).
- TLS versions: require TLS1.3 where available; fall back to TLS1.2 only with explicit tolerance documented.
- Cipher suites: prioritize AEAD suites (e.g., TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256).
- Revocation: support short lifetimes + online CRL/OCSP from local CA for emergency revocation.
- Bootstrapping: initial node provisioning uses a one-time bootstrap token validated by the platform account; token exchange happens over an isolated management channel.

RBAC v2: role definitions and network permissions mapping
- Motivation: separate human/operator privileges from automated bots and system identities controlling network constructs and firewall policies.
- Core roles (examples):
  - network-admin: can create/update firewall rules, route tables, and VPC peering for a deployment.
  - deployment-admin: can update deployment manifests, trigger rollout, request transient egress exceptions.
  - audit-reader: view audit logs, evidence bundles, SIEM export configurations (read-only).
  - evidence-bot: service identity that can collect artifacts, push to artifact store, and mark evidence snapshots as signed.

- Policy examples (high level):
  - network-admin restricted to resource-scope: /deployments/{deployment-id}/network/*
  - deployment-admin allowed: /deployments/{deployment-id}/manifest/* and /deployments/{deployment-id}/rollouts/* but NOT /deployments/*/network/*

- Enforcement points:
  - Console/API: all firewall changes must be made through Redwood's control plane API, which validates RBAC token scopes and emits an audit record.
  - IaC: changes from IaC pipelines must use service accounts with limited, auditable keys and a documented change window.

Audit log schema (flat, SIEM-friendly):
- timestamp (ISO8601)
- event_id (uuid)
- actor_id (user_id | service_id)
- actor_role (rbac role at time of event)
- action (string, e.g., firewall.update, cert.rotate, deployment.rollout)
- resource (resource path, e.g., /deployments/acme-prod/network/sg-123)
- resource_type (security_group|route_table|cert|deployment)
- outcome (success|failure)
- ip_source (ip or cidr)
- ip_destination (ip or cidr)
- request_agent (tool or sdk e.g., console, terraform, api-client)
- request_id (opaque id used for request tracing)
- change_summary (text description of what changed)
- diff_url (signed URL to a stored diff/artifact)

- Notes: prefer JSONL records with one event per line. Keep fields consistent for straightforward ECS mapping. Fields are intentionally flattened for SIEM parsers.

SIEM export best-practices:
- Export format: JSONL using the schema above. Prefer log forwarding (Fluent Bit/Fluentd) to HEC endpoints or to cloud-native log ingest (e.g., AWS Kinesis Firehose -> S3 -> SIEM).
- Timestamps: use UTC ISO8601 and include both event time and ingestion time.
- Integrity: sign periodic bundles (evidence snapshots) with a deployment-level key and include signature metadata in the audit record.
- Sample forwarder snippet (Fluent Bit-style minimal):
  [OUTPUT]
  Name  es
  Match  audit.*
  Host  telemetry-forwarder.local
  Port  9200
  TLS   On
  tls.verify  On
  tls.ca_file  /etc/forwarder/ca.pem
  tls.client_cert /etc/forwarder/cert.pem
  tls.client_key /etc/forwarder/key.pem

Evidence automation checklist (pipeline):
1) Trigger points: scheduled daily snapshot, pre-rollout, post-incident, or on-demand.
2) Artifacts to collect: active firewall rules, route tables, security group attachments, cert chain, CA fingerprint, RBAC bindings snapshot, audit.log slice (t-1h to t+1h), config diffs.
3) Packaging: create a compressed tar.gz with a manifest.json (manifest itself is a flat map), signature.asc (detached signature), and a metadata.txt with provenance.
4) Push: upload to customer-approved artifact store (S3 bucket with object lock/retention or on-prem artifact repo) and emit an audit event with diff_url pointing at the signed artifact.
5) Retention: align with customer retention policy; default evidence retention 90 days for infra snapshots, 365 days for signed compliance artifacts.

Hardening checklist (practical steps before go-live):
- [ ] Verify VPC segmentation: control, runtime, telemetry subnets exist and have ACLs configured.
- [ ] Ensure default-deny firewall posture and no wide-open 0.0.0.0/0 inbound rules for runtime subnets.
- [ ] mTLS enabled on all internal RPCs; cert rotation controller installed and exercised.
- [ ] RBAC v2 roles provisioned and validated with least privilege (no user is network-admin by default).
- [ ] Audit log forwarding configured and end-to-end tested; sample events visible in SIEM.
- [ ] Evidence automation run and signed artifact uploaded; diff_url resolvable.
- [ ] Egress paths inspected: no direct internet access unless explicitly approved through an egress proxy.
- [ ] Just-in-time tooling for emergency network changes documented and monitored.
- [ ] Pen test / tabletop exercise scheduled with networking team; results fed back into ruleset.

Operational runbooks (quick pointers):
- Emergency revoke: issue new CA intermediate, rotate certs for affected instances, mark revoked artifact in evidence store, and publish audit event with change_summary = "emergency CA rotate".
- Temporary egress exception: create a timeboxed rule with TTL tag, record ticket id in change_summary; automation should auto-revoke at TTL.
- Debugging connectivity: use certificate-validated curl (curl --cert client.pem --key client-key.pem) to test mTLS endpoints from platform bastion; always capture tcpdump and audit entries when troubleshooting.

Open questions / follow-ups (for this doc):
- Should customer-managed NGFW push rule-change webhooks to Redwood for automated diffing? (JIRA-INF-2482 tracks prototyping)
- Aligning evidence retention SLAs with legal/compliance; propose a templated SLO table per customer risk profile.

Appendix: Quick reference of recommended ports and identities
- 8443: control-plane API (mTLS) 
- 7100-7200: runtime RPCs (mTLS)
- 9200/443: telemetry ingestion (TLS + client cert)
- 22: management (bastion only, ephemeral/locked down)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft intended to be prescriptive but adaptable to customer needs. Please annotate with exact cloud-provider IaC snippets (Terraform modules) and any legal retention constraints you know of.
- Suggested reviewers: network-security, eng-sre, product-private-deployments.
